text:
Summary:
The short article explains how 2020–2022 “scaling-law” research by OpenAI and DeepMind revealed that, for a fixed compute budget, training smaller language models on proportionally larger datasets (the “Chinchilla” ratio) yields higher performance than continuing to grow parameter count alone. This overturns the earlier industry trend of unchecked parameter scaling. The text therefore presents a single, well-defined causal-interventional pathway: inefficient compute use (risk) → over-parameterisation (problem) → insight from empirical scaling laws → balanced-resource design rationale → concrete Chinchilla-ratio configuration mechanism → validation via Chinchilla vs Gopher experiments → actionable intervention: plan model size + dataset size with Chinchilla scaling before pre-training.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[78]
The fabric captures every explicit reasoning step and the only intervention that the data source either states or strongly implies. Confidence is reduced slightly by the absence of formal section headers and by some inference required to translate observed practice (“Chinchilla is better”) into an explicit intervention.

Inference strategy justification:
Where the article implies but does not explicitly label design rationale or intervention, moderate inference (edge-confidence = 2) was used, sign-posted in the edge and maturity rationales.

Extraction completeness explanation:
All distinct causal concepts in the text (risk, misallocation, theoretical scaling law, design strategy, implementation ratio, experimental validation) are represented; no other safety-relevant claims, methods, or findings are present; all nodes are interconnected and no duplicates remain.

Key limitations:
• Only one intervention could be derived; richer intervention sets would require external sources.
• Lack of headings required generic “main text” references in rationales.
• Empirical confidence is limited to a single research programme (DeepMind/OpenAI).
